advice: Don't trust a single energy reading of code that runs in under a millisecond.
detail: Hardware counters like Intel RAPL update roughly every 1 ms. Sub-millisecond workloads showed over 110% variation and often read zero.

advice: To measure a tiny function, run it many times in a loop and divide the total energy by the count.
detail: PowerLens repeats each code block 1,000 times so its energy rises above the counter's resolution.

advice: Lock the CPU frequency, disable Turbo Boost, pin to one core and stop background jobs before benchmarking energy.
detail: Frequency scaling and other processes otherwise leak into your readings.

advice: Repeat each energy measurement about 10 times, drop the outliers, and report the mean.
detail: With 10 trials and IQR outlier removal, over 90% of code blocks varied by less than 10% between trials.

advice: Let the hardware cool down between benchmark runs, and average across repetitions.
detail: HarmonE's experiments used five repetitions with a 20-minute cooldown between runs to keep hardware conditions stable.

advice: Sanity-check fine-grained energy numbers by confirming they add up to a whole-program measurement.
detail: Summed block-level readings closely matched whole-program energy, with much lower variance.

advice: Compare relative energy trends, not absolute joules, across different machines or measurement tools.
detail: Software meters like pyRAPL give Intel-specific estimates, so absolute values shift between platforms.

advice: Subtract an idle baseline and the model server's own energy to see what your framework really costs.
detail: The study records a 60-second idle reading per machine and tracks the model-serving process separately to isolate framework overhead.

advice: Use runtime and output tokens as quick proxies for an agent's energy; memory use tells you little.
detail: Energy correlated strongly with duration (R = 0.89) and output tokens (R = 0.88). Memory showed near-zero correlation because it is allocated upfront.

advice: Log LLM call counts and input/output tokens next to every energy reading.
detail: The volume of reasoning tokens can inflate energy independently of how well a framework orchestrates its work.

advice: Look at loop-heavy and deeply nested blocks first when hunting for energy hotspots.
detail: Loop count, conditionals, nesting and cognitive complexity all correlate with block energy across 18,000+ Python programs. Each link is weak on its own, so treat them as signals to check, not verdicts.

advice: Give blocks dense with arithmetic and other operators a closer look for energy cost.
detail: Operator density was the top-ranked feature in all three of EnCoDe's tree-based prediction models.

advice: Don't use cyclomatic complexity or code size alone as a stand-in for energy cost.
detail: Complexity metrics alone predicted energy tiers at 51% accuracy, which is barely above chance. Energy depends on how code features combine.

advice: Use static energy estimation to shortlist hotspots before you run anything, then confirm by measuring.
detail: Models trained on 33 static code features sorted blocks into low, medium or high energy with 80.6% accuracy. They're built for ranking hotspots, not exact joules.

advice: When refactoring a flagged block, compare the estimated energy of the old and new versions.
detail: EnCoDe's workflow flags high-energy blocks, then gives a comparative estimate between the original and refactored code to guide the choice.

advice: Keep your energy-analysis tooling lightweight too.
detail: A Gradient Boosting classifier used 0.015 J against Random Forest's 0.373 J for nearly identical accuracy (78.8% vs 79.2%).

advice: Compare agent frameworks on energy before adopting one; the architecture alone can swing usage 9×.
detail: On the same model and hardware, AutoCodeRover used 9.4× more energy per run than OpenHands.

advice: Track energy per successfully completed task, not per run.
detail: Small-model agents resolved almost no issues, so most of the energy they consumed bought nothing.

advice: Add loop detection: stop or change strategy when an agent repeats the same failing action.
detail: Small models kept resubmitting the same failing test script or malformed API call, and the frameworks never noticed.

advice: Filter and trim tool output before it reaches the model's context window.
detail: Broad grep commands returned huge unfiltered outputs that overwhelmed a 32K context and caused the agent to lose track.

advice: Never trust an agent's own "success" report; gate every generated patch on CI builds and tests.
detail: Frameworks reported success for destructive patches, such as replacing a 2,000-line file with a single invalid line.

advice: Treat suspiciously low agent energy as a possible early failure, not efficiency.
detail: Some low-energy runs ended early when the prompt exceeded the model's token limit, before any real work began.

advice: Budget for the orchestration loop, not just the model calls.
detail: Planning, memory, tool, reflection and retry cycles burn energy on every iteration, and agents often run for minutes or hours.

advice: Scan an agent framework's TODO, FIXME and HACK comments before betting production on it.
detail: Prior work found ML projects carry twice the self-admitted technical debt of non-ML projects. This study tests whether that debt also tracks energy use.

advice: Pin agent framework versions and re-measure energy after every upgrade.
detail: These frameworks change quickly, which is why the study compares releases several months apart.

advice: Prefer agent frameworks you can run locally and instrument; you can't optimise energy you can't observe.
detail: Observability and local deployability were selection criteria for the frameworks in the study.

advice: Keep a range of light to heavy models, and serve the lightest one that meets your accuracy target.
detail: HarmonE kept 95% of the heavy model's accuracy using 45.5% of its energy, and cut inference time by 53%.

advice: Check the energy cost of each candidate model before defaulting to the most accurate one.
detail: An LSTM reached R² 0.917 against an SVM's 0.821 for traffic forecasting, but used about 8.4× the energy.

advice: Benchmark energy across model sizes; the largest variant may cost 4× for a marginal gain.
detail: YOLOv8m used about 4.3× the energy of YOLOv8n for a 0.05 rise in mean detection confidence.

advice: Don't drop a small model into an agent framework built for large ones and expect savings.
detail: Swapping a small model in for a large one was found to be ineffective and often counterproductive. Current frameworks assume a capable reasoning engine.

advice: A smaller model can use more energy inside an agent loop; measure, don't assume.
detail: In two of four frameworks, Qwen-3 1.7B burned more tokens and energy than the larger Gemma-3 4B.

advice: Judge local models on total cost of ownership, not just the missing API bill.
detail: Local runs avoided API fees but some configurations averaged 24 to 27 minutes per issue.

advice: Retrain when data drift is detected, not on a fixed timer.
detail: Drift-triggered retraining used 54.5% less energy than an LSTM retrained on a fixed schedule.

advice: Before scheduling regular retraining of a heavy model, check that the accuracy gain is worth the energy.
detail: Periodic retraining added about 38% more energy to an LSTM for a gain of just 0.008 R².

advice: Store each model with the data distribution it was trained on, and reuse it when those conditions return.
detail: HarmonE checks its model repository for a matching past model before retraining, avoiding redundant work when familiar patterns recur.

advice: Pair model switching with selective retraining; switching alone drifts toward the heaviest model.
detail: Switch-only used more energy than HarmonE (24.3 vs 20.6 mJ) and still fell short of the heavy model's accuracy.

advice: Let the system adapt models to runtime conditions instead of always running the heaviest one.
detail: Adaptive operation kept about 97.5% of a static LSTM's accuracy with roughly 44% less energy.

advice: Set measurable accuracy, energy and drift thresholds at design time, and let them trigger actions.
detail: HarmonE turns sustainability goals into concrete limits, such as a maximum data-drift score before retraining.

advice: Monitor energy alongside accuracy and data drift in production, not accuracy alone.
detail: HarmonE's monitor combines accuracy, normalised energy and drift into one view of system health.

advice: Smooth your metrics and use tolerance bands so brief spikes don't trigger costly adaptations.
detail: HarmonE made 12 adaptations, against 17 for switching with periodic retraining.

advice: Don't let overhead worries stop you; a lightweight monitor-and-adapt loop costs very little.
detail: HarmonE's adaptation loop accounted for just 1.37% of total energy use.

advice: Keep adaptation logic in a separate control layer, outside your training and inference code.
detail: Harmonica wraps existing ML pipelines with an adaptation loop without changing how they train or serve.

advice: Store thresholds and adaptation policies in editable config, not hard-coded values.
detail: Harmonica keeps policies in JSON files that can be updated through a dashboard or API at runtime.

advice: Show energy and accuracy live against their thresholds so trade-offs are visible.
detail: Participants in Harmonica's user study named live telemetry the tool's strongest feature.

advice: Log every adaptation decision next to inference results so you can audit trade-offs later.
detail: Harmonica keeps historical logs of inference results and adaptation events for later analysis.

advice: Run a short pilot to confirm your candidate models really differ in accuracy and energy cost.
detail: HarmonE's pilot showed LR and SVM often performed well enough at far lower energy than an LSTM, which justified including them as candidates.

advice: Compare adaptive approaches against static, fixed-retraining and switch-only baselines on identical data splits.
detail: HarmonE compared nine approaches on the same splits, which exposed switching alone drifting toward the heavy LSTM.

advice: Inject controlled, repeatable drift that recurs, so you test both drift detection and model reuse.
detail: HarmonE applied the same scale-and-shift transformation to two test segments, so the data diverges and later returns to a familiar pattern.

advice: Fix hardware, precision, context window and timeout, and run every trial on an otherwise idle machine.
detail: SWEnergy ran all configurations in FP16 with a 32K context and a 30-minute timeout, each in isolation on one dedicated workstation.

advice: Repeat every task and configuration, using a representative benchmark subset if that's what makes repetition affordable.
detail: SWE-bench Verified Mini (50 tasks, about 5 GB instead of 130 GB) let SWEnergy run three full repetitions, 1,200 runs in total.

advice: Fix temperature, seed and prompts, do warm-up runs, reset state between trials, and pin tool versions.
detail: The study protocol uses temperature 0.0, seed 42, identical prompts, two warm-up runs against cold-start bias, and memory resets between trials.

advice: Run a small pilot that exercises the whole measurement pipeline before the main experiment.
detail: A 50-observation pilot must capture every metric, and any failure triggers reconfiguration before the 1,500-observation main run.

advice: Replicate on more than one hardware configuration, and only claim effects that hold on all of them.
detail: The study runs on three machines with different CPU generations and GPUs, and counts a hypothesis as supported only if all three agree.

advice: Select study subjects with written criteria, including whether they can run locally for direct measurement.
detail: Frameworks were screened for observability, local deployability and distinct architecture; a homogeneous pool would suppress the variance needed to detect correlations.

advice: Ablate feature groups, removing each and using each alone, before claiming any single metric explains energy.
detail: Complexity metrics alone reached R² = 0.067, barely above random, and no single group matched the full model.

advice: Compare Pearson with Spearman or Kendall, and check strong correlations against model feature importance.
detail: Rank correlations ran well above Pearson, revealing largely non-linear links; one feature with high rank correlation contributed little to prediction.

advice: Evaluate tools on more than one ML domain, and state plainly where your own approach was not applied.
detail: Harmonica ran time-series and object-detection pipelines, and says outright that HarmonE itself was not applied to the vision task.

advice: Have real users install and configure your research tool, and report what they found hard.
detail: Harmonica's 12-person study rated policy configuration lowest (4.08 out of 5) and surfaced a request for tooltips explaining tactics.

advice: Don't rely on single RAPL readings for code that runs in under about a millisecond.
detail: Below 1 ms, readings varied by more than 110%, and 4 to 5 of every 10 runs read zero.

advice: For tiny code blocks, amplify in a loop, start on a counter update, subtract padding energy, and filter repeated trials.
detail: With this PowerLens protocol, over 90% of blocks varied by less than 10% between repeated trials.

advice: Validate fine-grained energy measurements against a whole-program measurement tool.
detail: Summed block-level readings closely matched pyRAPL program-level energy across block types, with lower variance.

advice: Record each machine's idle power draw and subtract it from every energy trace you report.
detail: SWEnergy measured 51.69 W CPU and 2.70 W GPU at idle and removed it from all RAPL and NVML traces to isolate agent energy.

advice: Attribute energy by process ID to separate the inference server from the framework you're studying.
detail: Framework energy is planned as total energy minus the energy of the model-serving process, tracked by its PID.

advice: State exactly which components your energy tools cover; CPU and GPU totals are not whole-system energy.
detail: RAPL and NVML leave out RAM, storage and other motherboard components, so totals are not wall-plug energy.

advice: Measure the energy of your adaptation or monitoring logic itself, not just the system it manages.
detail: HarmonE's MAPE-K loop took 17.9 ms per invocation and 1.37% of total system energy.

advice: Repeat each configuration several times with cooldown gaps between runs before averaging energy.
detail: HarmonE used five independent runs with 20-minute cooldowns so temperature and background energy could settle.

advice: Log duration and token counts next to energy; in agent workloads they track it closely.
detail: Energy correlated with wall-clock duration (R = 0.89) and output tokens (R = 0.88), while memory showed near-zero correlation.

advice: Report energy together with task success, and verify outcomes independently of the system under test.
detail: The most frugal framework resolved 0% of tasks, and some reported successes were destructive or invalid patches.

advice: Report how skewed your outcomes are, and don't generalise per-success energy from a handful of successes.
detail: With near-zero resolution rates, SWEnergy notes its conclusions about failures are far more robust than those about successes.

advice: If an LLM helps analyse your logs, hand-check a random sample and publish the raw logs.
detail: SWEnergy used an LLM to classify failure modes, had two authors verify a random sample, and released the full logs.

advice: Pre-register hypotheses, statistical tests and support criteria before collecting data, for example as a registered report.
detail: Watts and Debts fixes its hypotheses, Spearman tests and significance level in advance as an ESEM registered report.

advice: With few units of analysis, fix a minimum effect size in advance and judge results by magnitude, not p-values.
detail: With only five frameworks, the study pre-specifies ρ ≥ 0.50 as the smallest effect worth reporting.

advice: Pin exact commits, and re-run on a later release to check whether your results still hold.
detail: Each framework is analysed at two snapshots months apart, with cross-version differences reported as limitations.

advice: Validate LLM-based labelling with an agreement threshold set in advance and a properly sized human-labelled sample.
detail: The classifier prompt is tuned to Fleiss's κ ≥ 0.80, then checked against 384 comments labelled by two independent reviewers.

advice: When energy values span orders of magnitude, report both absolute and relative error.
detail: EnCoDe's best regressor reached R² = 0.755 yet MAPE above 170%, driven by extremely low-energy blocks.

advice: Report the energy cost of your prediction model next to its accuracy.
detail: A Random Forest classifier used 0.373 J against XGBoost's 0.022 J, and was also slightly less accurate.

advice: Report which samples were too small to measure, and how many survived each filtering step.
detail: EnCoDe went from 18,612 files to 14,000+ executable blocks to 8,000+ above the 1 µs floor measurable at N = 1,000.

advice: Report accuracy, energy, latency and number of adaptations together so readers see the whole trade-off.
detail: HarmonE's results table shows all four for every approach, plus an energy-versus-error plot.

advice: Name your energy tool and its hardware limits, report the exact platform, and release code, configs and data.
detail: HarmonE notes pyRAPL works only on Intel processors, lists its full platform, and publishes its code and configurations.

advice: Package adaptation approaches as reusable exemplars rather than one-off case-study prototypes.
detail: Without exemplars, researchers must reimplement monitoring pipelines and adaptation logic, which limits reproducibility.

advice: Extend block-level energy estimation to varying input sizes and multi-threaded code.
detail: EnCoDe does not model how energy scales with inputs or runtime state, and pins measurement to a single core.

advice: Validate design-time energy estimation across languages and hardware, then move from detection to automated repair.
detail: EnCoDe covers Python 3.12 on one CPU; its authors call for other languages and runtimes and for actionable guidance.

advice: Build energy measurement that works across operating systems, virtual machines and mixed hardware.
detail: Harmonica calls consistent, portable energy instrumentation an open challenge, since pyRAPL is Intel-specific.

advice: Test sustainability-aware MLOps beyond time series, especially in vision, NLP and LLM-enabled systems.
detail: HarmonE was evaluated on one traffic-forecasting task; its authors highlight LLM and SLM systems, where model-selection trade-offs are sharper.

advice: Define domain-specific tactics so goal-driven adaptation works for computer vision pipelines.
detail: Harmonica suggests domain-specific MAPE-K files could extend the approach to vision tasks, but this has not been shown yet.

advice: Design agent frameworks for small models that detect loops, filter context and verify patches independently.
detail: SWEnergy argues current frameworks are passive orchestrators built for capable LLMs, and that SLMs need active management of their weaknesses.

advice: Test whether self-admitted technical debt can act as an early warning for energy-hungry frameworks.
detail: This is the hypothesis Watts and Debts sets out to test across five agentic frameworks; results are not in yet.
